2.intro: Modules are only useful if they change what you build. In this exercise you will write a complete, deployable instruction set for one agent — yours to choose — using every element from this module: identity, job, context, output format, boundaries, and escalation.

sections.heading: What you are producing
paragraphs: By the end of this worksheet you will have the full text of a system prompt: the standing instructions an agent would load before its first task. Not a sketch — the real thing, written the way you would hand it to a new employee whose judgment you cannot supervise minute to minute. Every field in the worksheet maps to a section of this module, so if a field feels hard to fill, that lesson is the one to revisit.

Choose an agent you genuinely care about. It can be the agent you designed in Lesson 1.5, a new one for your work, or a sharper version of an assistant you already use. Real stakes produce real instructions; a toy agent produces toy rules that teach you half as much.

sections.heading: How to fill each field
paragraphs: Identity and job (Lessons 2.1): keep the identity to two sentences; spend your words on the job, and end the job with its definition of done. Context sources (Lesson 2.2): name the actual sources — the document, the system, the record set — and add the rule for missing sources. Output format (Lesson 2.3): give the template or the fields; if a human reads it, use a template with the sections you would check for yourself.

Never list and escalation (Lesson 2.4): write behaviors, not topics, and give each escalation trigger a concrete line — an amount, a topic, a count of failed attempts. Finally, read your finished set once as if you were the agent meeting a strange case at 2 a.m. Whatever you find yourself unsure how to handle is the fallback rule you still need to write.

takeaways: A complete instruction set = identity + job with a definition of done + trusted context + output format + never list + escalation lines.
Write rules as behaviors with concrete triggers, not vague topics.
Test the draft against a strange case: gaps you find are the fallback rules still missing.
This instruction set is a build asset — Module 8's capstone will ask for its summary.

3.title: How APIs Work, in Plain Language
3.intro: Agents act through APIs, so this lesson removes the mystery: what an API request and response are, what endpoints and API keys do, and how to read an API the way you'd read a menu — no programming required.

sections.heading: A doorway built for software
paragraphs: A website is built for human eyes: layout, buttons, pictures. An API (Application Programming Interface) is the same service's doorway built for software: a program sends a precisely formatted request and gets precisely formatted data back — no screen, no clicking. When a weather app shows tomorrow's forecast, it asked a weather API. When your agent checks a calendar, it asks a calendar API.

The restaurant analogy holds up well: the dining room is the website, the kitchen is the service's real machinery, and the API is the waiter with a strict order form. You never enter the kitchen. You state exactly what you want in the form the waiter accepts, and exactly that comes back. This indirection is a feature: the service controls what can be asked for, by whom, and how often.

sections.heading: Requests and responses
paragraphs: Every API interaction is a pair. The request carries: where it's going (the endpoint — the specific 'door' for this kind of question, like /orders or /weather/forecast), what kind of action it is (read something, create something, update, delete), the parameters (which order? which city? which dates?), and proof of who's asking. The response carries a status — success or a specific kind of failure — plus the data asked for, in a structured format like JSON.

Statuses matter to agent builders because agents must react to them. A 200 means success. A 404 means 'that thing doesn't exist.' A 429 means 'you're asking too fast — slow down.' A 500 means the service itself broke. Lesson 3.4 is devoted to what agents should do with each; here the point is that failure arrives as information, not silence, and a well-built agent reads it.
bullets: Endpoint — the specific door for a kind of request (e.g. /flights/search)
Parameters — the specifics: which item, which dates, how many
Status — success (200) or a coded failure (404 not found, 429 too fast, 500 service error)
Response body — the data itself, structured (usually JSON)

sections.heading: API keys: the agent's ID badge
paragraphs: Services identify callers with API keys — long secret strings attached to each request, like an ID badge plus a signature. The key answers three questions for the service: whose account is this, what is it allowed to do, and how much has it used (for billing and rate limits). Your agent's tools hold keys so the agent itself never has to know them; the tool presents the badge when it knocks.

Treat keys like house keys, because that's what they are. A leaked key lets strangers use the service as you — spending your money and acting under your name. Rules that follow from this: keys live in the tool layer, never inside prompts (an agent can be talked into revealing what's in its context); different jobs get different keys where possible, so one leak doesn't open everything; and a key that may have leaked gets revoked and replaced immediately, which services make easy precisely because leaks happen.

sections.heading: Rate limits and the cost of asking
paragraphs: APIs ration requests: so many per minute, per day, per dollar. Rate limits exist because each request costs the service real resources, and they shape agent design more than newcomers expect. An agent that checks 10,000 records one request at a time may hit limits, run slowly, and cost real money; the same job designed around bulk endpoints finishes in a fraction of the calls.

This is why experienced builders read an API's limits and pricing before designing the agent around it. The questions are practical: How many calls will a typical task need? What does the service charge per call or per thousand? What happens at the limit — a queue, an error, a bill? An agent is a machine for making API calls; knowing the price of each call is knowing the price of the agent's work.

takeaways: An API is a service's software doorway: structured request in, structured data out — the waiter between your agent and the kitchen.
Requests carry an endpoint, an action, parameters, and identity; responses carry a status code plus data.
API keys are ID badges held by the tool layer — never placed in prompts, scoped per job, and revoked immediately if leaked.
Rate limits and per-call costs are design constraints: count the calls a task needs before you build it.

3.title: Designing Good Tools
3.intro: The model chooses tools by reading their names and descriptions — so tool design is really instruction design. This lesson covers the principles: one job per tool, names a stranger could guess, honest descriptions, and inputs and outputs shaped for the model that uses them.

sections.heading: One tool, one job
paragraphs: The single most useful rule in tool design: each tool does one well-defined job. get_order_status(order_id) is a good tool. manage_orders(action, ...) — which might look up, cancel, refund, or re-route depending on a mode flag — is four tools wearing a trench coat. The model must choose correctly every time, and a multi-mode tool makes every choice harder and every failure murkier.

Single-purpose tools are also easier to make safe. Permissions attach to tools: an agent allowed to look up orders but not cancel them simply doesn't receive the cancel tool. Split by job and you can hand out capabilities precisely; merge them and every grant is all-or-nothing. When you catch yourself adding an 'action' parameter that changes what a tool fundamentally does, split the tool.

sections.heading: Names and descriptions are the user interface
paragraphs: The model never sees your code. It sees a catalog: each tool's name, a description, and the input schema. Its choices are only as good as that catalog. Names should be verb-first and guessable by a stranger: search_flights, create_draft, refund_payment. If a smart newcomer couldn't predict what a tool does from its name, rename it.

Descriptions carry the judgment: when to use this tool, when not to, and what it returns. 'Searches the product catalog' is thin. 'Search the product catalog by keyword. Use for finding items to recommend; does not check stock — use check_inventory for availability. Returns up to 10 matches with prices' prevents real mistakes: the wrong-tool call, the assumed stock check, the surprise at result size. Write descriptions for the model the way you'd brief a capable new hire on their first day — because that's functionally what you're doing.
sections.example: Poor description: 'Gets customer data.' Good description: 'Look up a customer by email or account ID. Returns name, account tier, and open orders. Use before answering any account-specific question. Never returns payment details — those are not accessible to this agent.'

sections.heading: Inputs: make wrong calls hard
paragraphs: A tool's input schema is a form, and good forms prevent errors. Use precise types: a date field should be a date, not free text the model might fill with 'next Friday-ish.' Constrain choices with enumerated values where the real world has a fixed set (status: new | paid | shipped) rather than open strings. Mark genuinely required fields required, and give optional fields sane defaults so the model isn't forced to invent values.

Every input is also a validation opportunity. Your tool code should check ranges and formats the model proposes — a quantity of -3 or a date in the past for a booking gets rejected with a clear error the model can act on ('date must be in the future'). The model proposes; the tool disposes. A tool that trusts its inputs completely will eventually execute a confident mistake at machine speed.

sections.heading: Outputs: return what the next decision needs
paragraphs: Tool outputs go straight into the model's context, so they should be written for a reader who must decide what to do next. Return the fields the decision needs — not the service's entire raw record with forty irrelevant fields crowding the desk (Lesson 2.2 applies to tools too). Include status plainly, and make failures return their reason in words the model can relay or act on.

Consistency across your tool set multiplies reliability: same date format everywhere, same way of reporting 'not found,' same units. The model builds expectations across calls; a tool suite that behaves like one coherent product gets used correctly far more often than a pile of individually fine but mutually inconsistent tools.

takeaways: One tool, one job — split multi-mode tools so choices stay easy and permissions stay precise.
Names and descriptions are the model's only view of a tool: verb-first names, descriptions that say when to use it, when not to, and what comes back.
Input schemas are forms: precise types, enumerated choices, required fields marked, and server-side validation of everything the model proposes.
Outputs should contain what the next decision needs, in formats consistent across the whole tool suite.

3.title: Function Calling Step by Step
3.intro: You met function calling in Lesson 1.4. Now walk one complete call in slow motion — proposal, validation, execution, result, continuation — and see exactly where your code, not the model, holds the power.

sections.heading: The cast and the stage
paragraphs: Three parties take part in every function call. The model reasons and proposes. Your application (the harness around the model) validates, authorizes, executes, and records. The tool — often wrapping an API from Lesson 3.1 — does the actual work in the world. The model never touches the tool directly; everything passes through your harness, which is why the harness is where safety is built.

Set the scene: a support agent with tools get_order, create_refund, and send_reply. A customer writes: 'Order 58213 arrived damaged — I want my money back.' Watch what happens next, step by step, because this exact sequence is the heartbeat of every agent you will ever build or buy.

sections.heading: Steps 1–2: reason and propose
paragraphs: Step 1 — Reason: the model reads the message with its instructions in context. Its rules say refunds need the order verified first, and refunds over $50 need approval. It doesn't yet know the order's value, so its first move is a lookup, not a refund. Step 2 — Propose: instead of prose, the model emits a structured call: tool 'get_order', arguments {"order_id": "58213"}. Nothing has happened in the world yet — this is a request slip handed to the harness.

Notice what the model did not do: it did not decide it is allowed to refund, did not touch the payment system, and did not promise the customer anything. It identified the next piece of information the task requires and asked for it through the only channel it has. Good agents are, at this step, simply good at knowing what they need next.

sections.heading: Steps 3–4: validate, execute, return
paragraphs: Step 3 — Validate and authorize: the harness checks the proposal. Is 'get_order' in this agent's tool set? Is the argument well-formed? Is this agent permitted to read this customer's orders? Only then, Step 4 — Execute: the harness runs the tool, which calls the orders API with its key and gets back: order 58213, delivered, value $74, item: ceramic lamp. The harness logs the call (who, what, result) and hands the result to the model as an observation.

Now the loop turns with new facts. The model sees $74 — above its $50 approval threshold — so its next proposal is not create_refund but a prepared summary for a human: order verified, damage reported, refund of $74 ready to approve. If the value had been $30, it would have proposed create_refund, the harness would have validated that too, and the refund would have executed. Same machinery, different branch — the rules, not the mood of the model, decide which.
bullets: Propose — the model emits a structured tool call; nothing has happened yet
Validate — the harness checks the tool, the arguments, and the permission
Execute — the tool runs (usually an API call) and the result is logged
Return — the result enters the model's context as an observation; the loop continues

sections.heading: Parallel calls and chained calls
paragraphs: Two patterns complete the picture. When steps are independent, the model can propose several calls at once — check the weather in two cities, look up three orders — and the harness executes them in parallel, returning all results together. When steps depend on each other (you need the order before you can refund it), calls chain: each result informs the next proposal. Much of agent 'intelligence' in practice is just good chaining: never asking for step four's tool before step two's result is in.

And a quiet but crucial point: the model can also choose no tool at all. Answering a question from context, asking the user for a missing detail, or explaining that a task is outside its rules are all legitimate moves. A harness that forces a tool call every turn manufactures pointless actions; a model allowed to simply reply is an agent that can also hold a conversation.

takeaways: Every function call is: model proposes → harness validates and authorizes → tool executes → result returns as an observation.
The model never touches tools directly — your harness is where permission, validation, and logging live.
Rules decide the branch: the same machinery prepares an approval at $74 and executes a refund at $30.
Independent calls can run in parallel; dependent calls chain — and sometimes the right move is no tool at all.

3.title: Errors, Retries & Timeouts
3.intro: Real services fail: networks drop, servers overload, requests time out. This lesson covers how agents survive failure safely — which errors deserve a retry, which must never be retried blindly, and the plain-language idea of idempotency that keeps retries from double-charging anyone.

sections.heading: A field guide to failure
paragraphs: Failures arrive in families, and each family wants a different response. Transient failures — a dropped connection, a 500 from an overloaded server, a 429 asking you to slow down — are weather: they pass, and waiting then retrying is correct. Permanent failures — a 404 (the thing doesn't exist), a 400 (your request was malformed), a 403 (you're not allowed) — are facts: retrying the identical request will fail identically, forever. The agent's first job on any error is classification, not repetition.

Timeouts are the treacherous middle family: the request may have succeeded on the server while the response was lost coming back. A timed-out 'create payment' might mean no payment, or a payment you simply didn't hear about. Treating a timeout like a clean failure and retrying blindly is how double charges are born — which is exactly what the next section's concept prevents.

sections.heading: Safe retries: backoff and limits
paragraphs: A safe retry has three properties. It retries only transient failures. It waits between attempts — and waits longer each time (exponential backoff: 1 second, 2, 4, 8), because hammering a struggling service makes the struggle worse; a 429 response often even tells you how long to wait. And it has a hard limit — three or four attempts, after which the agent stops, records what happened, and escalates or reports failure honestly.

What an agent must never do is retry forever or retry instantly in a tight loop. Both convert a small outage into a self-inflicted denial-of-service and a large bill. Retry policy belongs in your harness and tool code — deterministic rules — not in the model's improvisation. The model should learn 'the tool failed three times' as an observation; it should never be the one deciding to try a fortieth time.
bullets: Transient (network drop, 500, 429): wait with backoff, retry a limited number of times
Permanent (400, 403, 404): do not retry unchanged — fix the request or escalate
Timeout: outcome unknown — verify state before any retry of a write

sections.heading: Idempotency, in plain terms
paragraphs: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Reading an order is naturally idempotent. Charging a card is not — two calls, two charges. Services make writes safe to retry with an idempotency key: a unique tag your harness attaches to the request ('refund-for-order-58213-attempt-1'). If the service receives the same key twice — because the first response was lost in a timeout — it recognizes the duplicate and returns the original result instead of charging again.

You don't need to implement this to use it: you need to know it exists, prefer tools and APIs that offer it for payments and other consequential writes, and follow one rule — after a timeout on a write, check the state first ('did that refund actually post?') before deciding what to do next. Verify, then retry if truly absent. That single habit eliminates the most expensive class of agent errors.

sections.heading: Telling the user the truth about failure
paragraphs: The last piece is communication. When part of a task fails after retries, the agent should say what succeeded, what failed, and what happens next — specifically. 'I booked the hotel and the airport transfer; the train booking failed after three attempts because the rail service is down, so I left it unbooked for you to retry later' preserves trust and lets the human act. 'Something went wrong' does neither.

Silent partial failure is the real enemy: an itinerary that looks complete but is missing its train, a report sent without the section whose data source was down. Design rule: an agent that cannot complete a step must surface that fact in its output — never paper over a gap with a plausible-sounding completion. In agent design, a loud failure is a success of the safety system; a quiet one is an accident in progress.

takeaways: Classify failures first: transient errors get backed-off, limited retries; permanent errors need a changed request or escalation.
Timeouts on writes are ambiguous — verify the actual state before retrying, and prefer tools with idempotency keys for consequential writes.
Retry policy (attempts, backoff, caps) lives in deterministic code, not in the model's improvisation.
Agents must report partial failure specifically — what succeeded, what failed, what's next — and never silently paper over gaps.

3.title: Read vs Write Tools & Approvals
3.exerciseIntro: Classify an agent's tools using the risk ladder from this lesson. Your answers save to your profile.

exerciseFields.label: 1. This agent's read tools (observe only — runs freely)
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Read inbox, search listings, check calendar, look up order status

exerciseFields.label: 2. Its prepare tools (drafts and staged actions — reversible)
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Create email draft, build a cart, draft a report — nothing sent or bought

exerciseFields.label: 3. Write tools that require your approval first
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Send email, place order up to $100, publish post — each prepared for me to confirm

exerciseFields.label: 4. Actions this agent must never have — tools you refuse to give it
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. No access to payment methods at all. No delete. No messaging customers directly.

3.intro: Lesson 1.4 drew the safety line between reading and writing. This lesson turns it into a working system: a four-rung risk ladder for tools, approval gates that humans actually enjoy using, and how an action earns promotion from gated to automatic.

sections.heading: The risk ladder
paragraphs: Not all write actions are equal, so one gate for everything is both unsafe and unusable. Sort every tool into four rungs. Rung 1 — Read: observe only (search, fetch, calculate); runs freely. Rung 2 — Prepare: creates reversible drafts and staged actions (a draft email, a filled cart, a proposed calendar hold); runs freely, because nothing has happened in the world yet. Rung 3 — Commit with approval: sends, buys, books, publishes, deletes — prepared by the agent, executed only after a human confirms. Rung 4 — Never for this agent: actions excluded entirely, because no benefit justifies their risk in this deployment.

The ladder's power is precision. Instead of debating whether an agent is 'safe' in the abstract, you debate one rung placement at a time: should sending a routine status email really sit on rung 3 forever? Should deleting records ever leave rung 4? Each placement is a small, revisable decision recorded in the design — and the set of placements is the agent's real safety policy.
bullets: Rung 1 — Read: runs freely
Rung 2 — Prepare: drafts & staging, reversible, runs freely
Rung 3 — Commit: executes only with human approval
Rung 4 — Never: the tool is not given to this agent at all

sections.heading: Designing approval gates people actually use
paragraphs: An approval gate fails in two directions. Too weak — a bare 'Approve?' with no context — and humans rubber-stamp it, which is worse than no gate because it manufactures false confidence. Too heavy — twenty approvals a day for trivia — and humans either disable the gate or approve without reading. A good gate presents the decision the way you'd want it at 8 a.m. with coffee: exactly what will happen, the key facts behind it, the cost or impact, and one-tap approve / reject / edit.

Batch and threshold thoughtfully. Routine, low-value, reversible commits can be batched into a single daily review; high-value or irreversible ones deserve their own immediate gate. And every gate decision is data: log approvals and rejections, because the rejection pattern tells you what the agent still gets wrong — which is the input to the next section.
sections.example: Good approval prompt: 'Send refund of $74 to customer M. Alvarez for order 58213 (damaged lamp, delivered Oct 18)? Policy limit without approval: $50 — this exceeds it because the item is fragile-class.' The human learns the amount, the reason, and why they're being asked — in one glance.

sections.heading: Earning autonomy: promotion with evidence
paragraphs: Autonomy should be earned per action, with evidence. The promotion path: an action starts on rung 3. Over a defined period — say 30 consecutive approvals with zero edits and zero rejections — it has demonstrated the agent prepares it correctly. You may then promote that specific action, within limits, to automatic execution: routine refunds under $25 auto-execute with logging, while everything above stays gated. The limits matter as much as the promotion: cap amounts, restrict scope (existing customers only), and keep the audit log permanent.

Demotion is the other half of the contract, agreed in advance: a single bad automatic execution sends the action back to rung 3 pending review. This is not punishment; it's the thermostat working. Teams that pre-agree promotion and demotion rules avoid the two failure modes of agent operations — never trusting anything (and drowning in approvals) or trusting everything after one good week (and meeting rung-4 consequences on a rung-3 budget).

sections.heading: The worksheet: your agent's ladder
paragraphs: The worksheet below applies the ladder to an agent of your choosing — ideally the same agent you've been designing since Lesson 1.5. List its tools on each rung. The exercise's real value is in rungs 3 and 4: deciding, in writing and in advance, what will always need your eyes and what you refuse to automate at all. Those two lists, honestly written, are most of an agent's safety case.

If you find a tool that doesn't fit a rung, that's a design smell — usually a multi-purpose tool from Lesson 3.2 that should be split (a 'manage message' tool becomes read_inbox on rung 1, draft_reply on rung 2, send_reply on rung 3). Split it, place the pieces, and the ladder goes back to being easy.

takeaways: Sort every tool onto a four-rung ladder: Read (free), Prepare (free, reversible), Commit (human approval), Never (not given).
Approval gates must present what will happen, the key facts, and the impact — rubber-stamping and approval fatigue are both gate failures.
Autonomy is earned per action with evidence (e.g. 30 clean approvals), promoted with limits, and demoted on the first bad execution.
If a tool won't sit on one rung, split it until its pieces do.

4.title: Short-Term vs Long-Term Memory
4.intro: The model remembers nothing between calls — so every agent's memory is a system you design. This lesson separates the two kinds: working memory for the task in front of the agent, and stored memory that persists across days, and explains why confusing them causes real failures.

sections.heading: Two kinds of memory, two different jobs
paragraphs: Short-term (working) memory is everything about the current task: the conversation so far, the goal, the steps taken, the tool results gathered, the drafts in progress. It lives in the context window — the desk from Lesson 1.2 — and it vanishes when the session ends. Its job is coherence right now: the agent should never ask for a fact it was given three steps ago or repeat a search it already ran.

Long-term memory is what persists: stored facts written to a database or files outside the model — user preferences, past decisions, completed work, learned corrections — retrieved into context when relevant. Its job is continuity across time: the agent that greets a returning customer already knowing their sizes, their last order, and that they hate phone calls, is running on long-term memory someone designed.

sections.heading: Why both exist
paragraphs: Neither substitutes for the other. Keep everything in working memory and the desk overflows: context windows are finite, cost grows with every token, and clutter degrades performance (Lesson 2.2). Store everything long-term and retrieve nothing, and the agent is a goldfish with a filing cabinet — the knowledge exists but never reaches the moment of decision.

The architecture that works is a loop between the two: working memory holds the active task; at meaningful moments, the system writes durable facts down to long-term storage; at the start of a task (and at decision points within it), the system retrieves the relevant stored facts back onto the desk. What gets written down, and what gets retrieved when, are design decisions — the subject of Lessons 4.2 through 4.4.
bullets: Working memory: current task, in context, fast, temporary, finite
Long-term memory: stored facts outside the model, retrieved on demand, persistent
The craft: deciding what to write down, and what to bring back, at which moments

sections.heading: What belongs where: a practical sorting rule
paragraphs: Sort by lifespan and by use. Anything needed only to finish the current task — intermediate results, the plan's checked-off steps, a document being summarized — is working memory only; persisting it is hoarding. Anything that would change how a future task should go — a preference, a decision and its reason, a correction the user made, a commitment the agent gave — is a candidate for long-term storage.

A useful test: imagine the user returns next week with a related request. What would you be annoyed the agent had forgotten? That list is your long-term memory design. What would you be annoyed it still remembered (a one-off address for a gift, a temporary instruction for a single day)? That list is your forgetting design — Lesson 4.4 takes it up directly.

sections.heading: Failure modes of each kind
paragraphs: Working memory fails by overflow and by loss: long tasks push early facts off the desk (the agent 'forgets' the original constraint by step 30), and sessions end mid-task with nothing saved. The mitigations are state summaries and checkpoints — Lesson 4.2. Long-term memory fails differently: it accumulates stale facts (the address from two moves ago, retrieved with total confidence), contradictions (two stored preferences that disagree), and things that should never have been stored at all.

Notice the asymmetry: working-memory failures are usually visible (the agent obviously lost the thread), while long-term failures are silent and confident — the agent acts on a stored 'fact' that stopped being true. That asymmetry is why long-term memory needs governance: dates on facts, sources, and review — not just storage.

takeaways: Working memory = the current task in context (fast, finite, temporary); long-term memory = stored facts retrieved when relevant (persistent, governed).
The architecture is a loop: write durable facts down at meaningful moments; retrieve them back at decision points.
Sort by the next-week test: store what would annoy the user if forgotten; plan to forget what would annoy them if kept.
Working memory fails loudly; long-term memory fails silently and confidently — it needs dates, sources, and review.

4.title: Conversation State & Summaries
4.intro: Long tasks outgrow the desk. This lesson covers the two standard solutions: keeping an explicit state record the agent updates as it works, and compressing history into summaries — plus the discipline of what a good summary must never lose.

sections.heading: State: the agent's checklist outside its head
paragraphs: Conversation state is a structured record of where a task stands, kept outside the chat transcript: the goal, the constraints, the steps completed, the steps remaining, the key facts discovered, the decisions made and by whom. Unlike the transcript — a river of text the model must re-read and reinterpret — state is a form: short, current, and unambiguous.

Keeping state explicit buys reliability in exactly the situations where agents wobble. When a session is interrupted and resumed, state is what makes resumption possible. When a task is handed to a different agent or a human (Module 6), state is what gets handed. And when something goes wrong, state is the audit trail that shows where. Many production 'agent' failures are really transcript-dependence failures: the knowledge existed only as vibes inside a long conversation.

sections.heading: Summaries: compression with judgment
paragraphs: When working memory fills, the standard move is summarization: the model compresses the older portion of the interaction into a shorter text that replaces it in context. Done well, this is how agents work on tasks far longer than any context window — a day of research becomes a page of findings, decisions, and open questions that the next phase works from.

Done badly, summarization is where facts go to die. Compression loses exactly the details the summarizer judged unimportant — and its judgment is the model's, not yours. Numbers get rounded or dropped, names blur, a tentative hypothesis hardens into a stated fact, and the caveat that mattered disappears. The control is a summarization spec: instruct what must survive verbatim (figures, dates, names, commitments, unresolved questions, anything flagged uncertain) and what may be compressed.
sections.example: Weak summary: 'We discussed the venue options and the customer seemed happy with the plan.' Spec-following summary: 'Venue: Riverside Hall confirmed for Oct 30, $1,800, deposit due Oct 10 (unpaid). Customer (M. Alvarez) approved the menu but NOT the bar package — decision pending her reply. Open: parking capacity for 120 guests unconfirmed.'

sections.heading: When to summarize, when to store raw
paragraphs: Summarize narrative; store facts. The story of how the agent explored options compresses beautifully. The facts the task depends on — IDs, amounts, addresses, the customer's exact words in a complaint — should be written to state or long-term storage verbatim, not trusted to a summary's mercy. A good rule: anything another step will quote, charge, book, or send must exist somewhere as exact data, with the summary merely pointing at it.

Timing matters too. Summarize at natural boundaries — a phase completes, a subtask closes — rather than mid-thought when the context alarm rings. Boundary summaries are written with the phase's outcome known, which makes them shorter and truer. Panic summaries written under token pressure are where the deposit date becomes 'sometime in October.'

sections.heading: State as a user-visible asset
paragraphs: A final, underused idea: show the state to the user. A small panel — goal, progress, key facts, pending approvals — turns the agent from a black box into a collaborator. Users catch errors early ('that's the old address') precisely because state is inspectable, and trust grows when people can see what the agent believes. If your agent's beliefs can't survive being displayed, that's diagnostic information about the design.

State also disciplines your design work. When you cannot write down, in a handful of fields, what your agent needs to track for its job, the job itself is not yet understood. The state schema is the job description in data form — design it with the same care as the system prompt.

takeaways: State is a structured record outside the transcript — goal, constraints, steps, facts, decisions — that makes tasks resumable, handable, and auditable.
Summaries compress narrative well and facts badly: specify what must survive verbatim (figures, dates, names, commitments, uncertainties).
Store facts as exact data; let summaries point at them. Summarize at phase boundaries, not under token panic.
Visible state builds trust and catches errors early — if the agent's beliefs can't be displayed, the design isn't finished.

4.title: Retrieval & RAG Without the Jargon
4.intro: How does an agent answer questions about a 500-page manual it can't fit on its desk? Retrieval: find the right pages first, then answer from them. This lesson explains retrieval and RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) in plain language, including what 'meaning search' really is.

sections.heading: The open-book exam
paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation — RAG — sounds technical and is actually simple: instead of asking the model to answer from memory, you first search your documents for the passages relevant to the question, place those passages in the model's context, and ask it to answer from them. It's an open-book exam where a librarian fetches the right pages just before each question.

This one pattern powers most 'chat with your documents' products and most knowledge-grounded agents. Its virtues are the virtues of grounding from Lesson 2.2: answers traceable to sources, knowledge that updates the moment you update the document (no retraining), and an agent that can say 'the manual doesn't cover that' because it can see what the manual actually says.

sections.heading: How the librarian finds pages: meaning search
paragraphs: Classic keyword search matches words: ask for 'refund' and you get pages containing 'refund' — but not the page that says 'money back within 30 days,' which is the page you needed. Modern retrieval adds embeddings: a way of converting text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so passages with similar meanings land near each other numerically even when they share no words. Your question is converted the same way, and the system fetches the passages nearest in meaning.

Say it plainly: embeddings are meaning coordinates. 'How do I get my money back' and 'refunds are issued to the original payment method' end up as neighbors, so the librarian fetches the returns policy when you ask about money back. This is why RAG systems can feel uncannily smart about your documents — and why they sometimes fetch a passage that's about the right topic but the wrong specifics, a failure mode we'll handle below.
bullets: Chunk: documents are split into small passages, each converted to meaning coordinates
Retrieve: the question's coordinates find the nearest passages (usually 3–10)
Generate: those passages go into context; the model answers from them

sections.heading: Chunking: how you slice decides what you find
paragraphs: Documents must be split into chunks before they can be indexed, and the slicing matters enormously. Too small and a chunk lacks the context that makes it meaningful ('…is not permitted' — what isn't?). Too large and the chunk dilutes: the answer hides inside three pages of neighbors, and the desk fills with mostly-irrelevant text. The working default is chunks of a few paragraphs, split at natural boundaries — headings, sections — with a little overlap so sentences aren't severed mid-thought.

Structure helps retrieval help you: documents with clear headings, descriptive titles, and dated versions retrieve better than walls of text, because chunks carry their headings as signposts. If your agent keeps missing answers that are definitely in the manual, suspect chunking and document structure before you suspect the model.

sections.heading: Where RAG fails, honestly
paragraphs: Retrieval fails in three recurring ways. The right passage isn't fetched (a retrieval miss) — the answer then gets invented or refused, depending on your grounding rules; refusing is the safe direction. The wrong-but-similar passage is fetched, and the agent answers confidently from the wrong policy section — the reason agents should cite which passage they used, so a human can spot-check. Or the passages are fetched but stale — last year's manual still indexed — which is a governance failure, fixed by versioning your sources, not by better models.

And know RAG's boundary: it finds passages, not answers that require combining a hundred facts, doing arithmetic across a spreadsheet, or reasoning over a whole database. Those jobs want tools (Module 3) or structured data access, not a better librarian. Choosing retrieval for the right problems — 'what does our documentation say about X' — is most of using it well.

takeaways: RAG = retrieve the relevant passages first, then answer from them: an open-book exam with a librarian.
Embeddings are meaning coordinates — search by similarity of meaning, not just shared words.
Chunking (a few paragraphs, natural boundaries, slight overlap) and clear document structure decide retrieval quality.
RAG fails by missing the passage, fetching a similar-but-wrong one, or serving stale sources — citations and versioning are the controls.

4.title: What to Store, What to Forget
4.intro: An agent that remembers everything is a liability with a search box. This lesson covers memory governance: what earns storage, what must never be stored, consent and sensitivity, and retention rules that delete on schedule instead of someday.

sections.heading: Memory is a liability as well as an asset
paragraphs: Every stored fact is three things at once: a future convenience, a future error waiting for the world to change, and a record you are responsible for protecting. Builders feel the first vividly and the other two vaguely — until the agent cheerfully tells a customer their old address, acts on a preference the user disowned years ago, or surfaces something sensitive in the wrong context.

The design stance that avoids most trouble: storage must be earned. A fact goes into long-term memory because it passed a test — it will plausibly matter again, it is stable enough to trust later, and storing it is appropriate for the person it concerns. Facts that fail any leg of the test stay in working memory and die with the session, which is the correct fate for most of what an agent sees.

sections.heading: What earns storage
paragraphs: Store preferences that recur (communication style, formats, standing constraints). Store decisions with their reasons — the reason is what makes the decision reusable when circumstances shift. Store corrections the user made to the agent's work; they are the highest-value training signal you will ever get, and re-making a corrected mistake is the fastest way to lose a user's trust. Store commitments and open loops: what the agent promised, what is owed, what is being waited on.

Every stored fact should carry its papers: when it was learned, from what source, and — for anything that can change — a review or expiry expectation. A preference from yesterday outranks one from two years ago, and the agent can only apply that logic if the dates exist. Undated memory is how two-year-old facts win arguments they should lose.
bullets: Store: recurring preferences, decisions + reasons, user corrections, commitments and open loops
Every fact carries: date learned, source, and a freshness expectation
When facts conflict, the newer dated fact wins — and the conflict gets flagged

sections.heading: What must never be stored (or stored only under strict rules)
paragraphs: Some categories demand a default of no. Credentials and secrets — passwords, keys, tokens — never enter agent memory; they live in dedicated vaults (Lesson 3.1). Sensitive personal data — health details, financial account numbers, precise location histories, information about third parties who never consented to your agent — should be stored only when the job genuinely requires it, with access limited to that job, and never because it was merely available.

Third-party information deserves special care. Your agent will read emails and documents full of facts about other people. 'The agent happened to see it' is not consent to build a dossier. A defensible rule: facts about the user, stored for the user's purposes; facts about others, used within the task that legitimately contains them and not retained beyond it — unless a human deliberately decides otherwise, in writing, for a stated purpose.

sections.heading: Retention: deletion as a scheduled behavior
paragraphs: Governance ends in a retention rule: how long each category of memory lives, and what deletes it. Task artifacts from routine jobs might live 90 days; preferences live until changed; session working memory dies at session end, always. The rule must be implemented — a job that actually runs — not aspirational text in a policy nobody executes. 'We delete after 90 days' that nobody coded is a promise the system makes and breaks daily.

Give users visibility and control proportionate to the stakes: a way to see what the agent remembers about them, correct it, and delete it. This is partly ethics, partly law in many jurisdictions, and entirely good engineering — the user is the world's best auditor of facts about themselves, and a correction interface turns them into your memory-quality team. Design the delete button before you design the store button; you will make calmer storage decisions.

takeaways: Storage must be earned: a fact must plausibly matter again, be stable enough to trust, and be appropriate to keep.
Store preferences, decisions with reasons, user corrections, and open loops — each with its date and source.
Never store credentials in agent memory; treat third-party facts as task-scoped, not dossier material.
Retention rules must be implemented as running deletion jobs, and users should be able to see, correct, and delete what's remembered.

4.title: Exercise: Design a Memory Plan
4.exerciseIntro: Design the memory for an agent of your choosing — the one you've been building through this course, or a new one. Your answers save to your profile.

exerciseFields.label: 1. Working memory — what must it track during a single task?
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. The current order being handled, steps done so far, the customer's stated preferences for this conversation

exerciseFields.label: 2. Long-term memory — what earns permanent storage, and why?
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Customer sizes and format preferences; decisions and their reasons; every correction a user makes

exerciseFields.label: 3. Retrieval — what knowledge sources will it search, and when?
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. The returns manual and past tickets, searched before answering any policy question; sources cited in the reply

exerciseFields.label: 4. Never stored — what must this agent refuse to keep?
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Card numbers, passwords, health details, facts about third parties beyond the task at hand

exerciseFields.label: 5. Retention & forgetting — what expires, when, and who can see/delete memory?
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Task notes deleted after 90 days; preferences kept until changed; user can view and delete everything stored about them

4.intro: Memory design is where agents earn the word 'assistant' — remembering the right things is what makes the second interaction better than the first. In this exercise you'll write a complete memory plan: what the agent tracks while working, what it keeps, what it searches, what it refuses to store, and what it forgets on schedule.

sections.heading: How to approach the plan
paragraphs: Work through the five fields in order; each maps to a lesson in this module. Working memory (4.1–4.2): list the state fields the agent must maintain mid-task — if you can't name them, the task isn't understood yet. Long-term memory (4.1, 4.4): apply the earn-storage test to each candidate fact and write down why it passes. Retrieval (4.3): name the actual sources — the manual, the ticket archive, the product database — and the moment in the workflow when each gets searched.

Then do the two fields builders skip. Never stored (4.4): write the refusal list before someone talks you out of it. Retention (4.4): give every category a number — days, or 'until changed' — and name who can view and delete the memory. A plan with no numbers in field 5 is a wish, not a retention policy.

sections.heading: A quality check before you save
paragraphs: Read your plan against two scenarios. Scenario one: the user returns after six months and the world has changed — new address, new preferences, a policy revision. Which of your stored facts could now be silently wrong, and does your plan's dating and sourcing let the agent notice? Scenario two: everything your agent stored is printed and handed to the user. Anything on that printout you'd be embarrassed to explain is a storage decision to reverse now, in the plan, rather than later, in an incident review.

takeaways: A memory plan has five parts: working state, long-term storage, retrieval sources, a never-store list, and retention rules with real numbers.
Stored facts need dates and sources so the agent can judge freshness and resolve conflicts.
Test the plan against the six-months-later scenario and the printout scenario before saving it.

5.title: Breaking Goals Into Steps
5.intro: Agents fail at big goals taken whole and succeed at the same goals taken in steps. This lesson teaches decomposition: how to break a goal into ordered, checkable steps, spot the dependencies between them, and know when a step is small enough.

sections.heading: Why decomposition is the core skill
paragraphs: Hand a model a large, tangled goal in one prompt and you get a plausible-looking rush: steps skipped, constraints honored early and forgotten late, no natural point to notice a mistake. Decompose the same goal into explicit steps and everything improves — each step is small enough to do well, its inputs and outputs are visible, and progress becomes a fact instead of an impression.

This mirrors how competent humans run projects, and for the same reasons. A plan externalizes the reasoning: instead of holding the whole task in the model's 'head' (its context, mid-generation), the steps sit in state (Lesson 4.2) where they can be checked, reordered, resumed, and audited. When you improve an agent's planning, you are mostly improving the artifact it plans on.

sections.heading: What makes a step the right size
paragraphs: A good step has four properties. It produces one clear output ('a shortlist of 5 venues with prices' — not 'research venues'). It can be verified on its own ('each venue states capacity ≥ 120' is checkable; 'good venues' is not). It uses one kind of work (searching, or deciding, or writing — a step that does all three will do the deciding implicitly and badly). And it is small enough that redoing it after a failure is cheap.

The test for 'small enough' is the failure test: if this step went wrong, would I want to redo just it, or would the damage force redoing everything around it? Steps that pass the failure test are the unit of safe progress. The most common planning flaw is the mega-step — 'plan the whole event' — which fails the test on every axis: unclear output, unverifiable, mixed work, expensive to redo.
bullets: One clear output per step
Verifiable on its own, against stated criteria
One kind of work per step: gather, decide, or produce
Cheap to redo if it fails

sections.heading: Dependencies and ordering
paragraphs: Steps connect: some cannot start until others finish (you can't compare venues before the shortlist exists), while others are independent and can run in any order or in parallel (booking the photographer doesn't depend on the menu tasting). Mapping these dependencies — even informally, as 'needs: step 2' on each step — is what turns a list into a plan. It prevents the classic agent error of executing in written order when the logic demands otherwise, like drafting the announcement before the decision it announces.

Ordering also follows risk: do the steps most likely to invalidate the plan early. If the whole event depends on one venue being available on one date, check that first — before the enjoyable, easy research that assumes it. 'Fail fast' in planning means sequencing so that bad news arrives while it's still cheap.

sections.heading: Plans the agent writes vs plans you give it
paragraphs: There are two sources of plans. Given plans: for repeated, well-understood jobs, you (the designer) write the steps once — a checklist the agent follows every time. This is maximally reliable and the right choice for production workflows. Agent-written plans: for novel goals, the agent decomposes at runtime, and you gain flexibility at the price of variance — the plan itself becomes something to review, at least for high-stakes tasks.

The professional pattern is a hybrid that grows over time: the agent plans freely at first, you review plans for important work, and every plan that proves itself gets saved as a template. Your template library is the agent's institutional knowledge — decomposition done once, correctly, and reused. In Lesson 5.5 you'll write one by hand, which is exactly how the library starts.

takeaways: Decomposition externalizes reasoning into checkable steps held in state — most agent reliability gains live here.
Right-sized steps: one clear output, independently verifiable, one kind of work, cheap to redo (the failure test).
Map dependencies ('needs: step 2') and sequence risky, plan-invalidating checks early — fail fast while it's cheap.
Save proven agent-written plans as templates; your template library becomes institutional knowledge.

5.title: Self-Checks & Verification
5.intro: The cheapest error is the one caught before it leaves the building. This lesson covers how agents check their own work: goal-criteria checklists, verification against sources, fresh-eyes review passes, and the difference between checking and merely re-reading.

sections.heading: Checking is a step, not a hope
paragraphs: Left unstructured, an agent's 'check' is a quick re-read that finds its own work convincing — models are notoriously generous graders of their own output, because the same plausibility engine that produced the answer evaluates it. Real verification is a designed step with its own instructions, its own criteria, and ideally its own angle of attack: verify against the goal's criteria, against the sources, and against the constraints — not against the agent's memory of what it intended.

The leverage is placement: a verification step costs one extra call and catches errors while they're still internal. Every error that escapes costs a correction conversation, a re-run, or a customer's trust. In any multi-step task you design from now on, budget the check explicitly — a plan without a verification step is a plan that assumes perfection, which is the one assumption this entire course argues against.

sections.heading: Check against criteria, not impressions
paragraphs: Verification needs something objective to check against, which is why well-formed goals carry criteria (Lesson 1.3: 'two options, before noon, under $400 including fees'). The check step converts each criterion into a yes/no question answered from evidence: Arrival before noon? — the itinerary says 11:40 ✓. Under $400 including fees? — $289 + $70 fees = $359 ✓. A criterion that can't be answered yes/no from the output and the sources is a criterion that was decorative; rewrite it.

Source-checking is the second axis: every factual claim in the output should trace to a tool result or document from this run. Claims that trace to 'the model just knows' get flagged — sometimes they're right, but flagged is the correct status until a source confirms them. This habit, automated, is what separates agents whose outputs can be trusted at a glance from agents whose outputs must be re-derived by a human every time (at which point the agent saved nothing).
sections.example: Verification output, done right: 'Checked against goal criteria — Options: 2 ✓ | Arrive before noon: 11:40 and 10:55 ✓ | Total under $400 incl. fees: $359 and $388 ✓ | Sources: flight search results + airline fee pages, this run ✓. One flag: the $359 option has a 45-minute layover — within your stated rules, but tight.'

sections.heading: Fresh eyes: changing the angle
paragraphs: Several techniques make self-checks sharper. The criteria pass: re-read the original goal and constraints fresh, then audit the output line by line (works because the goal text, not the output, drives the review). The adversarial pass: instruct the checker to argue why the output might be wrong — what would a skeptic attack? The recompute pass: for numbers, derive the result a second way (sum the line items instead of trusting the stated total). The sample pass: for bulk work, verify a random sample deeply rather than everything shallowly.

In bigger systems the checker becomes a separate agent (Module 6's Reviewer role) — a different model instance, sometimes a different model, with only the goal, the criteria, and the output in context. Separation helps because the checker doesn't inherit the worker's rationalizations. But even within one agent, a distinctly instructed check step captures most of the benefit. The non-negotiable part is that checking happens as its own act, with criteria in hand.

sections.heading: What happens when the check fails
paragraphs: A failed check is information, and the plan should say in advance what it's for: fix and re-check (bounded — two repair attempts, say), escalate to the human with the discrepancy described, or downgrade the claim (present the result with the unverified part clearly marked). What must never happen is the quiet edit — the agent 'fixing' a failed criterion by relaxing it ('45 minutes is basically before noon') — or simply not mentioning the failure. The check step's output is part of the record; hiding it converts a safety system into theater.

Track check failures over time and they become your improvement backlog: the criterion that fails every Friday is a rule that needs rewriting, a tool that needs fixing, or a goal template that was never realistic. Verification doesn't just protect today's task — it teaches you where your agent design is lying to you.

takeaways: Verification is a designed step with criteria — an unstructured re-read grades the agent's own work generously and catches little.
Check on two axes: every goal criterion answered yes/no from evidence, and every factual claim traced to a source from this run.
Sharpen checks with fresh angles: criteria pass, adversarial pass, recompute pass, sample pass — or a separate Reviewer agent.
Failed checks trigger a pre-decided response (bounded repair, escalate, or mark unverified) — never a quiet relaxation of the criterion.

5.title: When Plans Fail: Replanning
5.intro: Plans meet reality and reality wins arguments. This lesson covers the replanning skill: detecting that a plan has failed (versus merely wobbled), backtracking to the last good state, choosing a new route, and recognizing the point where the right move is to stop and escalate.

sections.heading: Detection: wobble vs failure
paragraphs: Not every surprise is a failed plan. A search returning weak results, one venue unavailable, a tool erroring once — these are wobbles the loop absorbs by adjusting a step. A plan has failed when its assumptions break: the required input doesn't exist, the constraint set is unsatisfiable (nothing arrives before noon under $400), a completed step's output turns out to be wrong, or the environment changed mid-task (the price moved, the file was deleted).

Agents are bad at noticing assumption failure because each individual step still 'works' — the searches return results, the drafts get written — while the plan quietly becomes impossible. The countermeasure is assumption-tracking: the plan states its load-bearing assumptions ('venue capacity ≥ 120 exists within budget'), and check steps (Lesson 5.2) test them explicitly. An assumption failing is a bright, designed signal — not a vibe the model must develop.

sections.heading: Backtracking to the last good state
paragraphs: When a plan fails, the amateur move is to patch forward from the wreckage; the professional move is to backtrack: return to the last step whose output is still valid, and replan from there. Because steps were designed to be verifiable and cheap to redo (Lesson 5.1), you usually know exactly which outputs survive: the research is still good, the shortlist criteria changed. Everything downstream of the broken assumption gets discarded or redone — including, painfully, completed work that was built on it.

Backtracking needs honest bookkeeping about what was real-world and what was draft. Drafts can be discarded freely. Committed actions — an email already sent, a booking already made — cannot be un-happened, only compensated (a correction email, a cancellation). This is yet another reason commits sit behind approvals (Lesson 3.5): a plan that fails before its approvals are granted fails cheaply, in the world of drafts.
sections.example: Plan failure: the only venue with capacity 120 is booked on the target date. Patch-forward: quietly shortlist venues of capacity 90 and hope. Backtrack: return to the step 'confirm constraints with the client,' surface the conflict — date vs capacity vs budget, pick two — and replan the shortlist step once the client chooses. The second path feels slower and is the only honest one.

sections.heading: Replanning well
paragraphs: A replan is a new plan, not a mood. It names what changed (the broken assumption), what survives (valid prior outputs), what the new route is (revised steps with their dependencies), and what it costs (steps, time, budget — Lesson 5.4's ledger continues, it doesn't reset). Writing this down in state matters because repeated replans are a diagnostic: a task replanned three times is telling you the goal, the constraints, or the tools are wrong, and that message should reach a human, not be absorbed by a fourth silent replan.

Cap the replans. A sane default: two substantive replans per task, then mandatory escalation with the full history attached. This isn't pessimism — it's the recognition that an agent grinding through plan after plan is burning budget to avoid delivering bad news, and bad news delivered early is a feature.

sections.heading: Knowing when to stop entirely
paragraphs: Some situations call not for a new plan but for a full stop: the goal itself turns out to be based on a false premise (the event was cancelled), pursuing it would now violate a rule (the only remaining route requires an unapproved action), or the human's intent is genuinely ambiguous in a way that changes the work fundamentally. Stopping well is a deliverable: what was attempted, what was learned, the exact blocker, and a specific question whose answer would restart the work.

Teach yourself to read an agent's stop as competence. Systems that never stop are not more autonomous; they're just less honest about the boundary of their mandate. The agents you can trust with bigger goals are precisely the ones whose stop-and-escalate behavior you've watched work on smaller ones.

takeaways: Distinguish wobbles (absorbed by the loop) from plan failure (a load-bearing assumption broke) — track assumptions explicitly so failure is a signal, not a vibe.
Backtrack to the last still-valid output and replan from there; discard downstream drafts, compensate committed actions.
A replan names what changed, what survives, the new route, and its cost — and replans are capped (two, then escalate).
Stopping entirely is a competence: deliver what was attempted, what was learned, the blocker, and the question that restarts the work.

5.title: Budgets: Steps, Time & Cost
5.intro: Every loop turn spends something. This lesson makes budgets a first-class design element: step caps, time limits, and token/dollar budgets — why they are safety features rather than accounting, and how to set numbers that are neither straitjackets nor blank checks.

sections.heading: The three currencies of a run
paragraphs: An agent run spends three currencies simultaneously. Steps: loop iterations and tool calls — each one a chance to act, err, or drift. Time: wall-clock minutes the user waits and services spend. Cost: tokens and API fees, which convert directly to dollars. A runaway in any one is a real incident: the agent that took 400 steps also took an afternoon and a noticeable slice of budget, usually to produce a worse result than step 40 would have.

Loops run away for mundane reasons: a success criterion that can never be satisfied ('keep improving the draft'), a tool that returns slightly different results each call so the agent keeps 'checking once more,' two instructions in quiet conflict, or a search space with no natural bottom. None of these announce themselves. The only reliable defense is that the budget exists in the harness, counts up relentlessly, and stops the run — budgets are enforced by code, never by asking the model to keep an eye on it.

sections.heading: Setting numbers that work
paragraphs: Set budgets from the task's shape, not from fear. A known workflow gets a tight budget: the weekly report agent needs ~15 steps; cap it at 25 and investigate any run that hits the cap — the cap is a smoke alarm, and smoke alarms that go off weekly get investigated, not disconnected. An open-ended research task gets a generous but finite budget, sized by the value of the answer: a question worth an hour of human time might justify 60 steps and $2 of tokens, stated in the task itself.

Make budgets visible in the run's output: steps used, elapsed time, approximate cost. Visibility changes behavior — yours first (you'll notice the task class whose cost crept up 10× after a tool change) and the design's second. A budget the user never sees is a budget nobody tunes.
bullets: Step cap — max loop iterations / tool calls per task
Time cap — max wall-clock duration before the run stops and reports
Cost cap — max tokens or dollars per task; counters live in the harness, enforced by code
Report usage with every result: steps, time, cost

sections.heading: Budgets as a safety feature
paragraphs: It is tempting to treat budgets as finance plumbing. They are, in fact, one of your four core safety mechanisms (with approvals, least privilege, and logging — Module 7). A malfunctioning or manipulated agent can only do damage at the speed of its loop; a step cap bounds the blast radius of every failure mode you failed to imagine, including the adversarial ones. An injected instruction that says 'email every contact in the address book' dies against a 25-step cap and a rung-3 send gate long before it becomes 400 emails.

Budgets also protect the agent from its principals' mistakes: the user who asks for 'every listing in the state, fully analyzed' has usually not priced that request. A budget converts an accidental five-thousand-dollar instruction into a conversation: 'This task as stated needs roughly 3,000 steps; here's a sampled version for 40 — shall I proceed with the full run?' That's not the agent refusing work; it's the agent surfacing the cost of the work, which is a professional courtesy in any trade.

sections.heading: Graceful exhaustion
paragraphs: What happens at the cap matters as much as the cap. The bad pattern: the run simply dies mid-step, leaving partial writes and no explanation. The designed pattern: as the budget nears exhaustion, the agent wraps up deliberately — commits nothing new, assembles the best current state of the work, and reports: what was completed, what remains, what the continuation would cost, and the state saved for resumption. Budget exhaustion becomes a checkpoint, not a crash.

Partial results delivered honestly at a checkpoint are worth more than complete results delivered never. Design the wrap-up into the instructions ('at 80% of your step budget, stop starting new subtasks and prepare your summary') and into the harness (a hard stop that still lets the agent write its final report). The report is exempt from the cap; the work is not.

takeaways: Runs spend steps, time, and cost simultaneously; runaway loops come from mundane causes and never announce themselves.
Budgets are enforced by harness code with hard caps, sized to the task's shape — and hitting a cap is a signal to investigate, not to raise silently.
Budgets are a safety mechanism: they bound the blast radius of malfunction and manipulation alike.
Design graceful exhaustion: near the cap, stop starting work, assemble state, and report what continuation would cost.

5.exerciseIntro: Plan a real task from your own work or life as an agent-ready 10-step plan, with verification and a budget. Your answers save to your profile.

exerciseFields.label: 1. The goal — with checkable criteria for “done”
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. Produce a comparison of 5 venues for a 120-person event on Oct 30, within $3,000, each verified for capacity and availability.

exerciseFields.label: 2. The 10 steps — one output each, dependencies noted (needs: step N)

1. Gather constraints from the client brief (output: constraint list)
2. Search venues in budget (needs: 1) (output: raw list)
3. Verify capacity ≥120 for each (needs: 2)…

exerciseFields.label: 3. The verification steps — what gets checked, against what criteria, at which points
exerciseFields.placeholder: e.g. After step 4: every price traced to a venue quote from this run. Final: all five goal criteria answered yes/no from evidence.
